paragraphs.en: What makes the problem thornier is that the usual time-management techniques don't seem sufficient. The web's full of articles offering tips on making time to read: “Give up TV” or “Carry a book with you at all times.” But in my experience, using such methods to free up the odd 30 minutes doesn't work. Sit down to read and the flywheel of work-related thoughts keeps spinning – or else you're so exhausted that a challenging book's the last thing you need. The modern mind, Tim Parks, a novelist and critic, writes, “is overwhelmingly inclined toward communication... It is not simply that one is interrupted; it is that one is actually inclined to interruption.” Deep reading requires not just time, but a special kind of time which can't be obtained merely by becoming more efficient.

paragraphs.en: In fact, “becoming more efficient” is part of the problem. Thinking of time as a resource to be maximised means you approach it instrumentally, judging any given moment as well spent only in so far as it advances progress toward some goal. Immersive reading, by contrast, depends on being willing to risk inefficiency, goallessness, even time-wasting. Try to slot it in as a to-do list item and you'll manage only goal-focused reading – useful, sometimes, but not the most fulfilling kind. “The future comes at us like empty bottles along an unstoppable and nearly infinite conveyor belt,” writes Gary Eberle in his book Sacred Time, and “we feel a pressure to fill these different-sized bottles (days, hours, minutes) as they pass, for if they get by without being filled, we will have wasted them.” No mind-set could be worse for losing yourself in a book.

paragraphs.en: So what does work? Perhaps surprisingly, scheduling regular times for reading. You'd think this might fuel the efficiency mind-set, but in fact, Eberle notes, such ritualistic behaviour helps us “step outside time's flow” into “soul time.” You could limit distractions by reading only physical books, or on single-purpose e-readers. “Carry a book with you at all times” can actually work, too – providing you dip in often enough, so that reading becomes the default state from which you temporarily surface to take care of business, before dropping back down. On a really good day, it no longer feels as if you're “making time to read,” but just reading, and making time for everything else.

sentences.reorder: 先译建议有效，再译 providing 的条件和 so that 的结果；from which 的抽身比喻拆成连续行为。
sentences.translation: “随时带着一本书”其实也能奏效——只要你翻阅得足够频繁，使阅读成为日常的默认状态，你只是暂时从中抽身出来处理事务，随后又回到阅读中。

words.meaning: 不定冠词，指一个或某一类；通常不单译
翻阅；短时投入阅读（dip in）
定冠词，限定所说对象；通常不单译
关系代词，指代前述事物
不定式标记，连接后面的动作；不单译
照管；处理（take care of）；关照
下来（sit down）；回到阅读状态（drop down）

auditV2.note: providing为只要，too为也，state为状态，take care of business为处理事务。

sentences.en: On a really good day, it no longer feels as if you're “making time to read,” but just reading, and making time for everything else.

chunks.en: On a really good day,
chunks.zh: 在状态特别好的一天

chunks.en: it no longer feels as if you're “making time to read,”
chunks.zh: 你不再觉得自己是在挤时间读书

chunks.en: but just reading,
chunks.zh: 而只是在读书

chunks.en: and making time for everything else.
chunks.zh: 需要另外腾出时间的是其他一切事情

sentences.reorder: no longer...but 保留感受的转变；末尾并列动作依中文改为“给其他事情腾时间”。
sentences.translation: 在状态特别好的一天，你不再觉得自己是在“挤时间读书”，而只是在读书，给其他一切事情另腾时间。

words.meaning: 不定冠词，指一个或某一类；通常不单译
与as组成仿佛／好像，而非条件如果
不定式标记，连接后面的动作；不单译
和；并且（连接并列或承接的内容）

auditV2.note: as if为仿佛，不是如果；把阅读变常态、其他事另腾时间的转变保留。

notes: 逐词重审阅读与时间工具化的比喻；纠正work、approach、state、physical、challenging等熟词生义，覆盖所有位置。
